segments.text: The goal is the manpage1 password, from /manpage/manpage0: a setuid manpage1 binary that calls setuid getuid, then strcpy's argv one into a 256-byte stack buffer.
The setuid getuid call drops the effective uid to manpage zero, but the saved set-user-id still holds manpage one, so a setresuid of seventeen thousand one regains the privilege.
The solve is a stack overflow with a shellcode.
I log in as manpage zero.

I measure the offset in gdb: the disassembly shows buf at e b p minus 0x100, so the saved EIP sits 260 bytes into the payload - two probes confirm it: 264 A's crash at 41414141, 260 A's plus BBBB crash at 42424242. gdb also shifts the stack, so the real address gets swept at run time.

The shellcode goes in vi first: twenty-four lines of nasm, setresuid of seventeen thousand one across all three uids, then execve of slash bin slash slash sh - assembled with nasm, forty-one bytes, no zero bytes. The exploit script follows in vi: NOP sled first, shellcode last, then the little-endian return address, swept around 0xffffd9e8 because the stack shifts with the environment.
Running the exploit sweeps candidate return addresses until the shellcode answers; the hit lands at 0xffffd5e0 and the spawned shell reads back the password file.
id confirms uid seventeen thousand one, manpage one.
And the password file reads back Mu eight G v M u d H b.
